# Draft Two Review 2026-07-08

Review of the second draft of The Salt Choir (the braid, about 118,000 words, sent 2026-06-12) with [[imogen-lacey|Imogen Lacey]] and [[callum-pryce|Callum Pryce]] on one video call. Wednesday, 14:00 to 16:10. Imogen had sent her [[imogen-editorial-letter-2026-07-03|letter on draft two]] five days before; Callum had sent his own [[callum-email-draft-two-2026-06-30|read]]. Daily context in [[recaps/daily/2026/2026-07-08|the recap for the day]].

## At a Glance

> [!note]
> Partial reversal of the February decision. Kept: three points of view, and Constance's chapters as letters. Reversed: the nonlinear braid; the book returns to chronological order, 1924 to 1929. The storm opening survives only as a four-page prologue. Callum dissented on the prologue and still does.

## Context

On the [[editorial-call-2026-02-19|editorial call of 19 February]] I chose a braid opening on the storm night. Draft two did what it promised structurally. The question for this call was whether it read.

## What Imogen said

From her letter and the call:

- Telling the storm first drained it. By the time the storm night returns in full in part three, the reader has had it in fragments five times and has worked out who is on the boat. The suspense the first draft lacked was not created, just spent earlier.
- Readers lost Tobias's war. His strand starts in 1924 but the war comes in pieces, inside storm-night sections and inside 1925 chapters, so the reader cannot tell which memory belongs to which year. Two of her colleagues who read it gave up on his timeline. [[tariq-mansour]]'s continuity notes found four places where his age or service dates conflicted ([[tariq-mansour-continuity-notes-2026-06-30]]).
- Constance's letters were the strongest thing in the draft.
- The three viewpoints are right. The town is now there.

## What I said

I had reached most of this myself on my own read-through in late June, which I should have done before sending ([[full-draft-read-through]]). I proposed: go back to chronological order, keep all three viewpoints and the letters, and keep a short prologue from the storm opening, so the reader knows from the first page that something will happen at sea. Imogen agreed, with one condition: the prologue must not tell the reader who dies.

## Callum's dissent

Callum argued against the prologue for about twenty minutes. His points:

- Any storm prologue tells the reader the lifeboat will be lost, and a reader who knows that reads parts one and two as waiting.
- The braid at least made the waiting the point; chronological order with a prologue keeps the spoiler without the design that justified it.
- Crime and thriller readers, which he thinks this book can reach, punish a given-away ending.

My answer: the prologue gives the reader a question, not an answer, if it stops before the boat comes back and names nobody. Imogen sided with me but said Callum's worry was "the right worry". We agreed to keep the prologue in the third draft and test it on first readers. It is unresolved: [[should-the-salt-choir-keep-the-storm-prologue]]; Callum restated it on 2026-09-17 ([[callum-prologue-call-2026-09-17]]).

## Decisions

- Third draft: chronological, three viewpoints, Constance's chapters as letters, prologue of no more than four pages ([[salt-choir-third-draft]], [[storm-prologue]]).
- Tobias's war in two whole remembered scenes, not fragments ([[how-much-of-tobiass-war-goes-on-the-page]]).
- Target 105,000 words.
- The braided rewrite is closed as superseded ([[braided-structure-rewrite]]).
- Delivery on 2026-09-30 is not realistic. Callum to raise a new date with Imogen; that became the [[delivery-date-extension]].

## Follow-ups

- Imogen's written summary arrived the next day ([[imogen-third-draft-brief-2026-07-09]]).
- Third draft planned and started 2026-07-13 ([[third-draft-planning-day-2026-07-13]]).
- Callum's position in writing: [[callum-email-on-prologue-2026-07-10]].
